meta.purpose: Ontology layer for cross-country taxonomy answers: framework profiles, a same-activity crosswalk, and a metric-by-metric comparison table.
how_to_use: profiles: load all of it for any cross-country question.

metrics.clusters: the same activity across frameworks with each framework's numeric thresholds, plus frameworks_with_no_numeric_threshold — say that explicitly rather than leaving a country out of the comparison.
crosswalk.links with status curated or confident are safe to state as 'the same activity'. status review means a human has not checked it — do not present those as equivalences.
frameworks.<id>.activities: full records for UMOA, Kyrgyzstan and the Philippines. EU and Korea activities come from their own files.
warnings: Compare structure BEFORE comparing strictness. A threshold framework and an activity-list framework cannot be ranked by strictness — one has no numbers.

Decimal separators differ. The EU and francophone documents use a comma as the decimal point (1,331 = 1.331); English-language documents use it as a thousands separator. Read the framework's decimal_separator before quoting any number.
Never cite an activity by its bare number. '4.5' means different activities in different EU annexes and in different frameworks. Always cite the full uid.

profiles.name: Green Finance Support Project Catalogue (2025 Edition)
profiles.issuer: People's Bank of China and co-issuing authorities
profiles.legal_basis: 绿色金融支持项目目录（2025年版）附件
profiles.structure_note_ko: 조건 칸에 숫자를 쓰지 않고 자국 표준(GB/GB-T 등)을 가리킨다. 숫자 비교가 성립하지 않고, '어떤 표준의 몇 급을 요구하는가' 까지만 비교할 수 있다.
notes: STRUCTURE: criteria point at Chinese national standards rather than stating numbers. Across 310 activities there are 247 distinct standard citations in 80 activities, against only 73 occurrences of a number with a unit. China therefore cannot be ranked numerically against the EU or Korea — what can be compared is which standard and which grade it demands (most often 1级能效, grade-1 energy efficiency).

The catalogue's own note 1: the policies and standards it cites are ADDITIONAL requirements. A supported project must still meet every other applicable law, regulation, and mandatory quality, safety, environmental, labour-protection and occupational-health standard, plus national and local industrial policy.

Nine fields, three of which no other framework in this dataset covers as classified categories: 绿色服务 (green services), 绿色贸易 (green trade) and 绿色消费 (green consumption, including purchase of new energy vehicles and of green low-carbon buildings by individuals).
Nuclear is included: 4.2.5 核电站及核能综合利用设施建设和运营 is marked as a direct carbon reduction activity.

There is no DNSH test and no minimum social safeguards chapter of the kind the EU, Korea and the ASEAN-lineage taxonomies have. Compliance with other law is required by note 1 instead. Say this plainly rather than implying China has a DNSH equivalent.

profiles.name: EU Taxonomy
profiles.structure_note_ko: 활동마다 수치 임계값이 규정에 박혀 있다. 다른 임계값형과 숫자를 직접 견줄 수 있다.
objectives_local: Sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources
Protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems
notes: One record per objective-activity pair: the Regulation states separate criteria per objective.
Minimum safeguards (Art. 18) are outside the delegated acts and are not in this dataset.

profiles.name: K-Taxonomy
profiles.issuer: Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (기후에너지환경부)
profiles.structure_note_ko: 활동마다 수치 임계값이 규정에 박혀 있다. 다른 임계값형과 숫자를 직접 견줄 수 있다.
notes: Korea places minimum safeguards inside the activity-level criteria; the EU keeps them outside the delegated acts (Regulation (EU) 2020/852 Art. 18), so EU activity records have no such field.
Korea's Transitional Area (전환부문, 7 activities) is recorded as activity_role=transitional.
Most exclusion criteria cross-refer to the guideline's attachments (붙임) rather than stating numbers inline, so few thresholds are extractable from them.

profiles.name: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy for Georgia
profiles.legal_basis: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy for Georgia (2022), Appendix
profiles.structure_note_ko: 활동마다 수치 임계값이 규정에 박혀 있다. 다른 임계값형과 숫자를 직접 견줄 수 있다.
notes: Produced with assistance from the European Union under the EU4Energy Initiative; the document states the contents are the sole responsibility of the National Bank of Georgia.
The Appendix is a proper activity table: Main Category | Category | Sub-category | NACE Code | Criteria/Technical Standard | Example/Explanation. 81 activities were recovered from it.

Criteria are visibly taken from the EU delegated acts — hydropower, for example, uses the EU's exact three-part test (run-of-river with no artificial reservoir, power density above 5 W/m2, or life-cycle GHG emissions below the threshold).
Uses NACE codes in the form D.35.11. Section letters follow NACE Rev.2 here.
The document also has a Green Taxonomy section and discusses mapping to international taxonomies and to sustainability objectives — so it positions itself as interoperable rather than independent.

profiles.name: Green Taxonomy of the Kyrgyz Republic (pilot national classifier)
profiles.legal_basis: Пилотный общенациональный классификатор – Зеленая таксономия Кыргызской Республики (2025), Приложение
profiles.structure_note_ko: 기술·장비·물품 단위까지 내려가고 관세 코드가 붙는다. 세제 혜택 집행 도구라서 '무엇이 녹색인가'보다 '무엇을 면세로 들여올 수 있는가'에 가깝다.
notes: The taxonomy is explicitly a PILOT: the document states the list of goods, activities and sectors will be expanded later.

Unlike the EU and Korea, rows go down to the level of equipment, goods and services, and each row carries customs codes (ТН ВЭД and EU CN Code) alongside industry codes. This is because the taxonomy is tied to tax relief — VAT exemption under Art. 191 §7.2 of the Tax Code, plus income-tax exemption for holders of green bonds listed on the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange.

The industry column is labelled NACE 2.1, a different edition from the NACE Rev.2 used by the EU delegated acts; section letters differ between editions, so only the numeric division+group is carried over to ISIC.
One record per technology (Технология). The rows beneath it — function groups and components — are kept in the 'components' field.

Objective is recorded as climate_mitigation for all records: the table has no per-row objective column, and the document's stated purpose is decarbonisation. Adaptation is named as an aim of the taxonomy but not mapped row by row. TO VERIFY: whether any rows should be classed as adaptation.

profiles.name: Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance
profiles.issuer: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS); developed by the Green Finance Industry Taskforce (GFIT), succeeded by the Singapore Sustainable Finance Association
profiles.legal_basis: Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance, 2023 edition
profiles.structure_note_ko: 활동마다 수치 임계값이 규정에 박혀 있다. 다른 임계값형과 숫자를 직접 견줄 수 있다.
objectives_local: Promote resource resilience and circular economy
notes: Only climate change mitigation has economic activities and technical screening criteria so far. The other four objectives are stated as future iterations — so a question about, say, Singapore's water criteria has no answer in this document yet.
62 activities were recovered from the document across Energy, Transport, Real Estate, Industry, Forestry, Carbon capture and storage, ICT, Waste, Water and Agriculture.
Explicitly designed to be interoperable with the EU Taxonomy and the ASEAN Taxonomy; many criteria cite 'EU Taxonomy' as their reference.

Of these, 36 are matched to their traffic-light criteria table and 26 are not — the pairing was only accepted where one criteria table belongs to exactly one activity. 11 criteria tables found no owner and are kept in 'unassigned_criteria'. classification.label: Green
classification.rule: Environmentally sustainable.

classification.label: Amber
classification.rule: Transition. Amber thresholds carry SUNSET DATES.

classification.label: Ineligible
classification.rule: Neither Green nor Amber. Note the third class is called 'Ineligible', not 'Red'.

assessment.method: Activities are defined on ISIC level 3. Criteria are set per activity as a traffic-light table (Green / Amber / Ineligible) with an interoperability reference, most often the EU Taxonomy.
assessment.dnsh_status: DNSH is currently BEST-PRACTICE DISCLOSURE in the early implementation phase, not an eligibility condition. The document says it could be incorporated into eligibility in future.
assessment.mandatory: Not mandatory and not contained in any regulation at the time of publishing; intended to be voluntary in its first years.

profiles.name: UMOA Taxonomy of green, social and sustainable projects
profiles.issuer: Autorité des Marchés Financiers de l'UMOA (AMF-UMOA)
profiles.legal_basis: Circulaire N°001-AMF-UMOA/2024 relative à la taxonomie des projets verts, sociaux et durables au sein de l'UMOA, §8.2
profiles.structure_note_ko: 적격 프로젝트 '목록'이다. 대부분의 항목에 수치가 없으므로, 임계값형과는 '같은 활동을 인정하는가'까지만 비교할 수 있고 '더 엄격한가'는 비교 대상이 아니다.
notes: This is NOT a threshold taxonomy. The Circulaire lists eligible projects per sub-category and tags each row with SDG icons and a mitigation/adaptation label. Only six numeric conditions appear anywhere in the tables; they are recorded as thresholds with the French source wording kept verbatim.
Criteria are recorded as type 'eligible_projects', not 'substantial_contribution': the document states what may be financed, not the performance an activity must meet.

The source PDF is a scan with no text layer and no French OCR model was available, so the tables were transcribed by reading the page images. Threshold wording is verbatim; some project lines are condensed — see raw/UMOA_transcription.md.
The freight-transport figures are quoted by the Circulaire from the Climate Bonds Standard, not set by AMF-UMOA itself.
Social projects carry no climate objective in the source table; they are recorded with objective='social'.
Jurisdictions: UMOA has 8 member states. The Circulaire applies union-wide.

profiles.name: ASEAN Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance
profiles.structure_note_ko: 정성 판단 틀(FF)과 수치 기준 틀(PS)을 함께 둔다. 같은 활동이 어느 틀로 평가되느냐에 따라 결과가 달라지므로, 비교할 때 어느 틀인지 먼저 밝혀야 한다.
objectives_local: EO3 Protection of healthy ecosystems and biodiversity
EO4 Resource resilience and the transition to a circular economy
notes: Tiers 2 and 3 will be gradually sunset over time for all Activities; the stated aim is to migrate every Activity to Tier 1. This is a designed expiry, not a grandfathering clause.

Annex 1 Activities sit in ISIC 351 (electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply), 352 (transmission and distribution of renewable and low-carbon gases, including storage) and 353 (heating/cooling production, including thermal storage), plus two activities that are not in ISIC at all: 000[010] Transport of CO2 and 000[020] Underground permanent geological storage of CO2.
Coal phase-out (CPO) is itself a classifiable Activity under the ASEAN Taxonomy.

The document states the ASEAN Taxonomy was the main reference for Indonesia's ITSF (OJK, 2025) and the Philippine SFTG (BSP, 2024). This is the stated lineage of the Philippine framework recorded separately in phl.json.
Version history stated in the document: V2 published 27 March 2023, effective 19 February 2024; V4 dated 6 November 2025.

classification.label: Green
classification.rule: Result in a positive benefit to one or more Environmental Objectives, or create utility while displacing a provider of that utility which detracts from an EO. Green-FF under the Foundation Framework; Green-Tier 1 under the Plus Standard.

classification.label: Amber
classification.rule: Amber-FF under the Foundation Framework; Amber-Tier 2 and Amber-Tier 3 under the Plus Standard. An Activity is classified Amber if it is causing or may cause significant harm.

classification.label: Red
classification.rule: Not aligned with the ASEAN Taxonomy.

frames.name: Foundation Framework
frames.note: Qualitative, sector-agnostic screening criteria and a decision flow. No numeric thresholds. Yields Green-FF or Amber-FF.

frames.name: Plus Standard
frames.note: Technical Screening Criteria for 6 focus sectors and 3 enabling sectors, in Tiers 1-3. Yields Green-Tier 1, Amber-Tier 2, Amber-Tier 3.

focus_sectors: Electricity, Gas, Steam and Air Conditioning Supply
Water supply, Sewerage, Waste Management and Remediation

profiles.jurisdiction_note: The ASEAN Taxonomy applies across ASEAN Member States. It is recorded here for the two AMS that have no national taxonomy of their own (Brunei, Myanmar); the other AMS are carried under their national frameworks, which the ASEAN Taxonomy sits alongside.

Sectors with technical screening criteria in the document include electricity generation and supply, minerals/mining and metals, manufacturing and industry, agriculture and land, construction and buildings, and transport.
Australia's mandatory climate DISCLOSURE regime (from 1 January 2025) is separate from the taxonomy, which is voluntary. Do not conflate the two.

profiles.name: Philippine Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines (SFTG)
profiles.legal_basis: BSP Circular No. 1187, Series of 2024 (Monetary Board Resolution No. 193, 14 February 2024), amending Sec. 153 of the Manual of Regulations for Banks
profiles.structure_note_ko: 활동 목록도 임계값도 없다. 분류 규칙과 유도질문으로 평가자가 판단한다. 비교 가능한 것은 분류 논리·목표 범위·피해 처리 방식이다.
future_objectives: Protection of healthy ecosystems and biodiversity
Promotion of resource resilience and transition to circular economy
notes: This is a principles-based taxonomy. There are no per-activity numeric thresholds to compare against the EU or Korea; what can be compared is the classification logic, the objectives covered, and the treatment of harm and transition.

The Amber class is the closest counterpart to Korea's 전환부문 (Transitional Area) and to the EU's transitional activities, but it works differently: the EU and Korea name transitional activities in advance with criteria attached, while the Philippines decides case by case on whether harm is remediable in time.

SOURCE TEXT QUALITY: the text available for this build came from OCR of a scanned circular and contains character errors. Nothing here is offered as a verbatim quotation. Any passage that needs to be quoted must be re-checked against the original PDF.
TO VERIFY: whether BSP has issued a born-digital version of the SFTG annex, which would allow verbatim extraction of Tables 7-12 (the guiding questions).

classification.label: Green
classification.rule: The activity makes a substantial contribution to an Environmental Objective and meets the Essential Criteria (DNSH and Minimum Social Safeguards).

classification.label: Amber
classification.rule: The activity makes a substantial contribution to an Environmental Objective but causes significant harm to another. It still qualifies if that harm can be remediated within 5 years, or an independent verification supports a claim that remediation will take less than 10 years, and the Essential Criteria of DNSH and MSS are met.

classification.label: Red
classification.rule: The activity does not serve any Environmental Objective or does not meet the Essential Criteria. A Red activity may still receive 'unlabelled' financing; the label does not imply the activity is unsustainable, only that it does not meet the SFTG's ambition.

essential_criteria.name: Do No Significant Harm
essential_criteria.note: An activity contributing substantially to one Environmental Objective must not significantly harm any other.

essential_criteria.name: Remedial Measures to Transition
essential_criteria.note: Measures that remove or render insignificant any actual or potential significant harm; specific time periods are allowed for an activity to become aligned. This is the mechanism behind the Amber class.

essential_criteria.name: Minimum Social Safeguards
essential_criteria.note: Compliance with national regulatory requirements, assessed at COMPANY level rather than activity level.

assessment.method: Guiding questions and a decision flow diagram, not numeric activity thresholds. The guidelines carry use cases for mitigation (Appendix 3) and adaptation (Appendix 4), a non-exhaustive list of Philippine laws for MSS (Appendix 1), and examples of industry standards and certifications (Appendix 5).
assessment.objective_choice: One Environmental Objective must be named as primary, even when both are listed.

profiles.applies_to: Banks — when extending credit, making investment decisions, and designing sustainable financial products and services
relationships: Certain definitions are borrowed and adapted from the ASEAN Taxonomy Version 2.
For sustainable bond issuance, banks follow the SEC's sustainable bond standards; the SFTG may be applied voluntarily on top of them.

msme_treatment.note: MSMEs are addressed separately. The Philippines defines MSMEs both by employment size (PSA) and by asset size (Magna Carta for MSMEs, as amended 2008); either may be applied under the SFTG.
msme_treatment.examples_source: IFC Sustainable MSME Finance Reference Guide
msme_treatment.examples_caveat: The guidelines state these are examples only and do not constitute automatic endorsement of alignment under the SFTG.

profiles.developed_by: Financial Sector Forum (FSF), following the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap issued by the inter-agency Green Force in October 2021

metrics_caveat: comparable=true only means more than one framework put a number on this activity. It does not mean the numbers measure the same thing — check each entry's metric, unit and verbatim text before saying one country is stricter.

metric_index.purpose: Every numeric threshold in the dataset, grouped by metric and value, so a question like 'which countries use 100 gCO2e/kWh?' can be answered directly.
caveats: Equal values do NOT mean equal criteria. The activity they attach to, the date they apply from, and the exceptions around them differ. Read each entry's verbatim text before saying two countries have the same rule.
A shared value very often means one framework copied the EU delegated acts. That lineage is worth stating, and it is also the reason the values match.

Percentage thresholds are NOT grouped by value: a percentage means something different in every criterion (emission savings, efficiency, recycled content, leakage reduction). They are listed per framework instead, under 'percent_by_framework'.
'kind' says whether the sentence reads as a taxonomy criterion or as national-policy context (an NDC target, for example). Only quote 'criterion' entries as thresholds.

crosswalk.method: ISIC group must match, then Jaccard similarity of normalised activity-name terms (Cyrillic transliterated, French and Russian function words dropped, synonyms folded to English); score >= 0.5 confident, 0.25-0.5 needs human review, below that weak. 'curated' links were checked by reading both names.
crosswalk.caveat: A link means the two frameworks describe the same kind of activity. It does NOT mean the criteria are equivalent — comparing the criteria is the point of the link. In particular a link between a threshold framework (EU, Korea) and an activity-list framework (UMOA, Kyrgyzstan) connects an activity to a project category, and only one side has numbers.

framework.name: ASEAN Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance
framework.jurisdiction_note: The ASEAN Taxonomy applies across ASEAN Member States. It is recorded here for the two AMS that have no national taxonomy of their own (Brunei, Myanmar); the other AMS are carried under their national frameworks, which the ASEAN Taxonomy sits alongside.

objectives.local: EO3 Protection of healthy ecosystems and biodiversity
EO4 Resource resilience and the transition to a circular economy

classification.label: Green
classification.rule: Result in a positive benefit to one or more Environmental Objectives, or create utility while displacing a provider of that utility which detracts from an EO. Green-FF under the Foundation Framework; Green-Tier 1 under the Plus Standard.

classification.label: Amber
classification.rule: Amber-FF under the Foundation Framework; Amber-Tier 2 and Amber-Tier 3 under the Plus Standard. An Activity is classified Amber if it is causing or may cause significant harm.

classification.label: Red
classification.rule: Not aligned with the ASEAN Taxonomy.

frames.name: Foundation Framework
frames.note: Qualitative, sector-agnostic screening criteria and a decision flow. No numeric thresholds. Yields Green-FF or Amber-FF.

frames.name: Plus Standard
frames.note: Technical Screening Criteria for 6 focus sectors and 3 enabling sectors, in Tiers 1-3. Yields Green-Tier 1, Amber-Tier 2, Amber-Tier 3.

focus_sectors: Electricity, Gas, Steam and Air Conditioning Supply
Water supply, Sewerage, Waste Management and Remediation

notes: Tiers 2 and 3 will be gradually sunset over time for all Activities; the stated aim is to migrate every Activity to Tier 1. This is a designed expiry, not a grandfathering clause.

Annex 1 Activities sit in ISIC 351 (electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply), 352 (transmission and distribution of renewable and low-carbon gases, including storage) and 353 (heating/cooling production, including thermal storage), plus two activities that are not in ISIC at all: 000[010] Transport of CO2 and 000[020] Underground permanent geological storage of CO2.
Coal phase-out (CPO) is itself a classifiable Activity under the ASEAN Taxonomy.

The document states the ASEAN Taxonomy was the main reference for Indonesia's ITSF (OJK, 2025) and the Philippine SFTG (BSP, 2024). This is the stated lineage of the Philippine framework recorded separately in phl.json.

assessment.method: Initial development phase covers climate change mitigation criteria for six priority sectors, plus a DNSH framework and Minimum Social Safeguards.
assessment.dnsh_structure: DNSH applies at ACTIVITY level and considers potential and actual impacts across the whole lifecycle of an asset, activity or project. It has two layers: generic criteria (principles-based, one set per environmental objective) and specific criteria (particular requirements).
assessment.mandatory: Voluntary. ASFI makes the initial taxonomy available for use by firms, investors and regulators on a voluntary basis; government review of it and of possible use cases was scheduled separately.

notes: Only climate change mitigation has substantial-contribution criteria; the other five objectives appear only as DNSH objectives. This is the same shape as Singapore and Fiji.

Sectors with technical screening criteria in the document include electricity generation and supply, minerals/mining and metals, manufacturing and industry, agriculture and land, construction and buildings, and transport.
Australia's mandatory climate DISCLOSURE regime (from 1 January 2025) is separate from the taxonomy, which is voluntary. Do not conflate the two.

• The infrastructure must support the diversion of at least 70% of waste from landfills by 2035.
• At least 50% of the processed waste, by weight, must be converted into secondary raw materials suitable for use in production processes.
• The facility must demonstrate the capability to handle at least 50% of recyclable materials coming from industrial, commercial, and municipal sources.
• Facilities must implement a system for continuous monitoring of the quantity of materials reused, ensuring at least 50% of materials processed by the facility are suitable for reuse.
• Leak detection and repair (LDAR) programs must be in place to prevent any contamination of reusable materials, and leakage rates must be kept below 5% of total processed materials.

• Facilities must achieve a minimum of 20% energy savings in wastewater treatment operations compared to a baseline year (utilizing energy-efficient technologies such as cogeneration or renewable energy sources) • Facilities should incorporate resource recovery processes, such as biogas generation from sludge, to ensure that at least 50% of the sludge is repurposed or converted into energy.

• Projects should employ Best Available Technologies (BAT) for wastewater recycling, including physical processes, biological processes, chemical process and further treatment options • At least 50% of treated wastewater must be reused or recycled in industrial processes, agriculture, or non-potable urban uses, reducing freshwater withdrawal by this percentage.
• The reuse system must integrate energy-efficient technologies, achieving at least a 20% improvement in energy efficiency from baseline operations.
• The facility must demonstrate a minimum 20% reduction in methane emissions.
• Methane emissions from the landfill and any leakage from the landfill gas collection systems must be controlled by a monitoring plan, ensuring leakages remain well below a 1% threshold.

• Incineration should only be considered for non-recyclable waste, and facilities must recover a minimum of 25% of the energy contained in the waste during incineration for electricity or heat generation.
• U-values at least 10% lower than minimum EE requirements (maximum allowable thermal transmittance coefficient, U max ), based on average weighted by external area of building element.

predecessor.name: Green Bond Endorsed Projects Catalogue (2021 Edition) 绿色债券支持项目目录
predecessor.issued: jointly announced by the People's Bank of China (PBOC), the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) on 21 April 2021
predecessor.note: The 2021 catalogue governs GREEN BONDS. The 2025 catalogue is broader — green FINANCE — so the two are not simply old and new versions of the same instrument. An English version of the 2021 catalogue exists; the 2025 one was read in Chinese.

notes: STRUCTURE: criteria point at Chinese national standards rather than stating numbers. Across 310 activities there are 247 distinct standard citations in 80 activities, against only 73 occurrences of a number with a unit. China therefore cannot be ranked numerically against the EU or Korea — what can be compared is which standard and which grade it demands (most often 1级能效, grade-1 energy efficiency).

The catalogue's own note 1: the policies and standards it cites are ADDITIONAL requirements. A supported project must still meet every other applicable law, regulation, and mandatory quality, safety, environmental, labour-protection and occupational-health standard, plus national and local industrial policy.

Nine fields, three of which no other framework in this dataset covers as classified categories: 绿色服务 (green services), 绿色贸易 (green trade) and 绿色消费 (green consumption, including purchase of new energy vehicles and of green low-carbon buildings by individuals).
Nuclear is included: 4.2.5 核电站及核能综合利用设施建设和运营 is marked as a direct carbon reduction activity.

There is no DNSH test and no minimum social safeguards chapter of the kind the EU, Korea and the ASEAN-lineage taxonomies have. Compliance with other law is required by note 1 instead. Say this plainly rather than implying China has a DNSH equivalent.

framework.issuer: Ministerio de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales
notes: Spanish-language document with criteria closely tracking the EU delegated acts — for example the water-supply criterion of closing the leakage gap by at least 20%, and material recovery from separately collected non-hazardous waste.
Uses 'Criterios de contribución sustancial' for substantial-contribution criteria.

ACTIVITY LIST NOT YET EXTRACTED. What IS here is every numeric threshold sentence found in the document, quoted verbatim with its metric and unit, and marked as a criterion, as national-policy context, or as ambiguous. Quote only the ones marked 'criterion' as taxonomy thresholds.

thresholds.verbatim: República Dominicana, en su NDC 2020, aumenta su ambición climática al comprometerse a la reducción de un 27 % de las emisiones de GEI con respecto al BAU o “Business as Usual” al 2030. Éste con un objetivo de un 20 % condicionado a finanzas externas y un 7 % incondicionado a finanzas domésticas, siendo este distribuido en un 5 % correspondiente al sector privado y un 2 % al sector público.

El país propone lograr, a partir de opciones de mitigación evaluadas y propuestas, reducir 13,853.71 Gg CO2eq lo que representa 27.16 % con respecto al escenario BAU 2030 estimado en 51 mil Gg CO2eq, con una inversión requerida estimada de USD $8,916,950,000.00 expresada de forma condicionada e incondicionada.

La actividad reduce la brecha en al menos un 20%, entre el nivel de fugas actual promediado durante tres años, calculado utilizando el método de clasificación del Índice de Fugas de Infraestructura (ILI) y un ILI de 1.5, o entre el nivel de fugas actual promediado durante tres años, calculado utilizando otro método adecuado. b.

Criterios de contribución sustancial La recuperación de material de residuos no peligrosos, recogidos ya separados, está alineada directamente, siempre y cuando cumpla con los siguientes criterios: ● Esta actividad garantiza la conversión de al menos el 25% del total de los residuos no peligrosos procesados, con planes para aumentar esta cifra al 50% en un período de tres años.

Este criterio está sujeto a revisión periódica. ● Las actividades relacionadas con la captura de emisiones en las instalaciones (p.e.j.: procesos industriales que emiten GEI excepto de los procesos relacionados con la extracción y uso de combustibles fósiles), siempre que garanticen la captura de al menos el 60% (hasta el año 2030 como un criterio de transición) y después debe garantizar la captura de al menos 90% de las emisiones de GEI generadas en los procesos industriales, están alineadas.

La actividad cumple con los siguientes criterios: ● El CO2 transportado desde la instalación donde se captura hasta el punto de inyección no da lugar a fugas de CO2 superiores al 0.5% de la masa de CO2 transportada. ● Se aplican sistemas de detección de fugas adecuados y se cuenta con un plan de monitoreo, con el informe verificado por un tercero independiente.

Del mismo modo, la República Dominicana, mediante la actualización en el año 2020 de su Contribución Nacionalmente Determinada (NDC-RD 2020), se comprometió a una reducción del 27% de los gases de efecto invernadero para el año 2030.

Se trata de un tipo de energía renovable, inagotable y no contaminante que puede producirse en instalaciones que van desde los pequeños generadores para autoconsumo con potencia instalada menor a 1 MW 49 hasta las grandes plantas fotovoltaicas.

50 Para el caso de República Dominicana, la capacidad instalada en sistemas solares fotovoltaicos al cierre del año 2023 es de 675.08MW, que corresponde al 11.9% del total de la capacidad instalada en la matriz energética del país [5,675.12 MW].
thresholds.decimal_warning: comma present: this document's decimal convention must be checked before the value is used in arithmetic. EU-derived criteria use the comma as a decimal point (0,0072 = 0.0072).

Para el caso de República Dominicana, la capacidad instalada de hidroeléctricas es de 623.28 MW, que corresponde al 11% del total de la capacidad instalada en la matriz energética del país [5,675.12 MW].

Generación de gran escala, con potencia instalada mayor a 10 MW (o con reservorio): ● La densidad de potencia de la instalación de generación de electricidad es superior a 5 W/m2. o ● Las emisiones de GEI del ciclo de vida de la generación de electricidad a partir de energía hidroeléctrica son inferiores a 100 gCO2e/kWh.
Estableciendo un criterio de potencia superior a 5W/m2 o emisiones inferiores a 100gCO2e/kWh en su ciclo de vida, asegura que la actividad es eficiente y está alineada con otras taxonomías.
59 Criterios de contribución sustancial Las emisiones de GEI del ciclo de vida de la generación de energía a partir de la fuente geotérmica deben ser inferiores a 100 gCO2e/ kWh.
Por eso, es importante demostrar que las emisiones de GEI son inferiores a 100gCO2e/kWh en su ciclo de vida para que estén alineados.

El metano extraído se emplea para producir energía térmica, mecánica o simplemente eléctrica Criterios de contribución sustancial Todas las instalaciones deben demostrar que operan con emisiones de ciclo de vida inferiores al umbral vigente (100 gCO2e/kWh), por medio del cumplimiento de la ISO 14067 o de un producto del protocolo de GEI, como el Product Carbon Footprint (PCF).

Al establecer un umbral de emisiones inferior a 100gCO2e/kWh y requerir que la biomasa provenga de fuentes sostenibles, se garantiza que la generación de bioenergía contribuya efectivamente a la mitigación del cambio climático sin comprometer los ecosistemas ni la seguridad alimentaria.

Más del 67% de la capacidad de generación recientemente habilitada en el sistema está por debajo del valor umbral de generación de 100 gCO2e/kWh medido sobre la base del ciclo de vida de acuerdo con los criterios de generación de electricidad, durante un período de cinco años continuo. b.

El factor de emisiones de la red del sistema promedio, calculado como las emisiones anuales totales de la generación de energía conectada al sistema, dividido por la producción de electricidad neta anual total en ese sistema, está por debajo del valor umbral de 100 gCO2e/ kWh en su ciclo de vida de acuerdo con los criterios de generación de electricidad, durante un período de cinco años móviles.

Construcción y operación de la conexión directa, o expansión de la conexión directa existente, de generación de electricidad con bajas emisiones de carbono por debajo del umbral de 100 gCO2e / kWh medido sobre la base del ciclo de vida a una subestación o red. b.
La energía del distrito térmico permite una transición lejos del uso de combustibles fósiles y puede resultar en una reducción del 30-50% en el consumo de energía primaria.

Criterios de contribución sustancial Las emisiones de GEI del ciclo de vida de la generación combinada de calor/frío y energía de la energía geotérmica son inferiores a 100 gCO2e/kWh en la generación combinada.

70 Criterios de contribución sustancial Todas las instalaciones deben demostrar que operan con emisiones de ciclo de vida inferiores al umbral vigente (100 gCO2e/kWh), por medio del cumplimiento de la ISO 14067 o de un producto del protocolo de GEI, como el PCF.
Criterios de contribución sustancial La fabricación de hidrógeno está alineada si las emisiones de GEI en su ciclo de vida son iguales o inferiores a 3 tCO2e/t de hidrógeno.

Como alternativa, el proyecto puede demostrar que la fuente de energía utilizada tiene emisiones de GEI inferiores a 100 gCO2/kWh en su ciclo de vida, cumpliendo así con los criterios establecidos para el sector de energía en la taxonomía.
La intensidad media de carbono de la energía de estos sistemas debe ser igual o inferior a 100 gCO2/ kWh durante la vida útil de la infraestructura.
Si se utiliza una planta desalinizadora, la energía utilizada para los sistemas debe tener emisiones de menor o igual 100gCO2 e/KWh (umbral del sector de energía).

framework.name: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy for Georgia
notes: Produced with assistance from the European Union under the EU4Energy Initiative; the document states the contents are the sole responsibility of the National Bank of Georgia.
The Appendix is a proper activity table: Main Category | Category | Sub-category | NACE Code | Criteria/Technical Standard | Example/Explanation. 81 activities were recovered from it.

Criteria are visibly taken from the EU delegated acts — hydropower, for example, uses the EU's exact three-part test (run-of-river with no artificial reservoir, power density above 5 W/m2, or life-cycle GHG emissions below the threshold).
Uses NACE codes in the form D.35.11. Section letters follow NACE Rev.2 here.
The document also has a Green Taxonomy section and discusses mapping to international taxonomies and to sustainability objectives — so it positions itself as interoperable rather than independent.

framework.name: Ghana Green Finance Taxonomy (Phase One)

assessment.method: Technical screening criteria built on five pillars: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, environmental protection, resource efficiency and pollution prevention. DNSH and minimum social safeguards apply.
assessment.governance: A diverse stakeholder committee governs the taxonomy.

notes: PHASE ONE IS QUALITATIVE. The document states the rollout is phased: Phase 1 develops qualitative criteria for the selected sectors; Phase 2 introduces QUANTITATIVE THRESHOLDS, tax exemptions and sector-based incentives (stated target: May 2025); Phase 3 develops a transitional taxonomy covering carbon-intensive sectors such as oil, gas and mining. So a question about Ghana's numeric thresholds has no answer in this version — say so.
TO VERIFY: whether Ghana has since published the Phase 2 document with quantitative thresholds. This dataset holds Phase One only.

Aligned by the document with the Ministry of Finance's Sustainable Financing Framework, the SEC's Green Bond Guidelines, and the Bank of Ghana's Sustainable Banking Principles (with the Ghana Association of Banks and the EPA).

framework.name: Kenya Green Finance Taxonomy
notes: Builds on the CBK's Guidance on Climate-Related Risk Management issued in October 2021, which the taxonomy document describes as the step before it.

The document runs to about 128,000 characters and contains substantial-contribution and DNSH language throughout (52 and 18 mentions), but almost NO numeric units — zero gCO2e or tCO2e occurrences and only four percentage figures. Kenya's criteria are therefore qualitative, and a question about Kenya's numeric thresholds should be answered by saying the taxonomy does not set them, not by borrowing another country's numbers.

framework.name: Green Taxonomy of the Kyrgyz Republic (pilot national classifier)
notes: The taxonomy is explicitly a PILOT: the document states the list of goods, activities and sectors will be expanded later.

Unlike the EU and Korea, rows go down to the level of equipment, goods and services, and each row carries customs codes (ТН ВЭД and EU CN Code) alongside industry codes. This is because the taxonomy is tied to tax relief — VAT exemption under Art. 191 §7.2 of the Tax Code, plus income-tax exemption for holders of green bonds listed on the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange.

The industry column is labelled NACE 2.1, a different edition from the NACE Rev.2 used by the EU delegated acts; section letters differ between editions, so only the numeric division+group is carried over to ISIC.
One record per technology (Технология). The rows beneath it — function groups and components — are kept in the 'components' field.

Objective is recorded as climate_mitigation for all records: the table has no per-row objective column, and the document's stated purpose is decarbonisation. Adaptation is named as an aim of the taxonomy but not mapped row by row. TO VERIFY: whether any rows should be classed as adaptation.

framework.name: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy for the Cambodian Banking Sector

classification.label: Green (aligned)
classification.rule: Substantial contribution to the specified environmental objective — either already at or near zero emissions, or on a clearly defined Paris-aligned decarbonisation pathway.

classification.label: Amber (transitional)
classification.rule: Not yet at or near net zero, but contributing to substantial emission reductions on a credible decarbonisation pathway towards the Green criteria. Subject to specific performance thresholds and SUNSET DATES, by which they must meet Green criteria to remain aligned. Equivalent to Tier 2 and Tier 3 of the ASEAN Plus Standard.

classification.label: Red
classification.rule: Not aligned.

assessment.method: Sectoral Decarbonization Approach (SDA), using IEA, IPCC and IIASA scenarios. The Green threshold follows the 1.5°C pathway; the Amber threshold follows the non-OECD NDC-based pathway (Transition Pathway Initiative, 2021).

notes: Dated April 2026 — newer than most national taxonomies in this dataset.

The document notes that technical screening criteria are often NOT defined for most waste management activities, and that numeric criteria are used where eligibility needs them (hydropower is the example given) and to draw the Amber/Red boundary.
Includes Annex 2 on the early and managed phase-out of coal-fired power plants, and Annex 3 a whitelist of activities.

framework.name: Philippine Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines (SFTG)
framework.legal_basis: BSP Circular No. 1187, Series of 2024 (Monetary Board Resolution No. 193, 14 February 2024), amending Sec. 153 of the Manual of Regulations for Banks
framework.developed_by: Financial Sector Forum (FSF), following the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap issued by the inter-agency Green Force in October 2021
framework.applies_to: Banks — when extending credit, making investment decisions, and designing sustainable financial products and services
future_objectives: Protection of healthy ecosystems and biodiversity
Promotion of resource resilience and transition to circular economy

classification.label: Green
classification.rule: The activity makes a substantial contribution to an Environmental Objective and meets the Essential Criteria (DNSH and Minimum Social Safeguards).

classification.label: Amber
classification.rule: The activity makes a substantial contribution to an Environmental Objective but causes significant harm to another. It still qualifies if that harm can be remediated within 5 years, or an independent verification supports a claim that remediation will take less than 10 years, and the Essential Criteria of DNSH and MSS are met.

classification.label: Red
classification.rule: The activity does not serve any Environmental Objective or does not meet the Essential Criteria. A Red activity may still receive 'unlabelled' financing; the label does not imply the activity is unsustainable, only that it does not meet the SFTG's ambition.

essential_criteria.name: Do No Significant Harm
essential_criteria.note: An activity contributing substantially to one Environmental Objective must not significantly harm any other.

essential_criteria.name: Remedial Measures to Transition
essential_criteria.note: Measures that remove or render insignificant any actual or potential significant harm; specific time periods are allowed for an activity to become aligned. This is the mechanism behind the Amber class.

essential_criteria.name: Minimum Social Safeguards
essential_criteria.note: Compliance with national regulatory requirements, assessed at COMPANY level rather than activity level.

assessment.method: Guiding questions and a decision flow diagram, not numeric activity thresholds. The guidelines carry use cases for mitigation (Appendix 3) and adaptation (Appendix 4), a non-exhaustive list of Philippine laws for MSS (Appendix 1), and examples of industry standards and certifications (Appendix 5).
assessment.objective_choice: One Environmental Objective must be named as primary, even when both are listed.

msme_treatment.note: MSMEs are addressed separately. The Philippines defines MSMEs both by employment size (PSA) and by asset size (Magna Carta for MSMEs, as amended 2008); either may be applied under the SFTG.
msme_treatment.examples_source: IFC Sustainable MSME Finance Reference Guide
msme_treatment.examples_caveat: The guidelines state these are examples only and do not constitute automatic endorsement of alignment under the SFTG.

relationships: Certain definitions are borrowed and adapted from the ASEAN Taxonomy Version 2.
For sustainable bond issuance, banks follow the SEC's sustainable bond standards; the SFTG may be applied voluntarily on top of them.
notes: This is a principles-based taxonomy. There are no per-activity numeric thresholds to compare against the EU or Korea; what can be compared is the classification logic, the objectives covered, and the treatment of harm and transition.

The Amber class is the closest counterpart to Korea's 전환부문 (Transitional Area) and to the EU's transitional activities, but it works differently: the EU and Korea name transitional activities in advance with criteria attached, while the Philippines decides case by case on whether harm is remediable in time.

SOURCE TEXT QUALITY: the text available for this build came from OCR of a scanned circular and contains character errors. Nothing here is offered as a verbatim quotation. Any passage that needs to be quoted must be re-checked against the original PDF.
TO VERIFY: whether BSP has issued a born-digital version of the SFTG annex, which would allow verbatim extraction of Tables 7-12 (the guiding questions).

framework.name: Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance
framework.issuer: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS); developed by the Green Finance Industry Taskforce (GFIT), succeeded by the Singapore Sustainable Finance Association

objectives.local: Promote resource resilience and circular economy

classification.label: Green
classification.rule: Environmentally sustainable.

classification.label: Amber
classification.rule: Transition. Amber thresholds carry SUNSET DATES.

classification.label: Ineligible
classification.rule: Neither Green nor Amber. Note the third class is called 'Ineligible', not 'Red'.

assessment.method: Activities are defined on ISIC level 3. Criteria are set per activity as a traffic-light table (Green / Amber / Ineligible) with an interoperability reference, most often the EU Taxonomy.
assessment.dnsh_status: DNSH is currently BEST-PRACTICE DISCLOSURE in the early implementation phase, not an eligibility condition. The document says it could be incorporated into eligibility in future.
assessment.mandatory: Not mandatory and not contained in any regulation at the time of publishing; intended to be voluntary in its first years.

notes: Only climate change mitigation has economic activities and technical screening criteria so far. The other four objectives are stated as future iterations — so a question about, say, Singapore's water criteria has no answer in this document yet.
62 activities were recovered from the document across Energy, Transport, Real Estate, Industry, Forestry, Carbon capture and storage, ICT, Waste, Water and Agriculture.
Explicitly designed to be interoperable with the EU Taxonomy and the ASEAN Taxonomy; many criteria cite 'EU Taxonomy' as their reference.

thresholds.verbatim: Singapore has aimed to reduce emissions to around 60MtCO2e in 2030 after peaking emissions earlier and committed to reach net-zero emissions by 2050.
For example, Singapore has a set the target of reducing peak land transport emissions by 80% by 2050 from the 2016 peak, with vehicle electrification as the main driver.

As also highlighted earlier, an explicit goal of the City in Nature vision under the Singapore Green Plan is to implement species recovery plans for 100 species of plants and 60 species of animals, restore 30 hectares of forest, marine, and coastal habitats, and enhance habitats in at least 50% of Singapore’s gardens, parks, and streetscapes.9 6Source:
On food supply, Singapore’s 30 by 30 goal intends to meet 30% of nutritional needs locally by 2030, up from less than 10% today.

Singapore aims to achieve the solar target of at least 2GWp by 2030 (which will constitute around 3% of the country’s total protected electricity demand in 2030).
Singapore Singapore has committed to meet a net zero target by 2050 and has enhanced its NDC to reduce emissions to around 60MtCO2e in 2030 after peaking emissions earlier.
For new projects, this means that the green threshold is at 100gCO2e/kWh to bring the grid average down rapidly.
This threshold drops to 50gCO2e/kWh to 2050.
For amber thresholds, this is based on the TPI energy modelling above where the 2030 threshold for 2°C scenario is at 220gCO2e/kWh for grid average.

The rationale for the 220gCO2e/kWh in the short term would be to import electricity that has significantly low enough average emissions than the current grid as to act as a lever for significant emissions reduction to decarbonise the grid average in the short.

For e.g., CCGTs that secures financing from 2029 need to be 50% hydrogen-ready at the onset. *However, the proposed threshold of 100% vol from 2033 is intended to be read as forward guidance for countries like Singapore which are alternative energy disadvantaged.

For 2033-2035, the deployment of new 50-100% hydrogen-ready CCGT would be provided as a forward guidance by EMA, based on when we expect utility-scale units to be available with acceptable reliability, efficiency, and baseload compatibility with natural gas.

For CCGTs that had secured financing before the thresholds were ratcheted up in 2029 and 2033, the plants will have to demonstrate that they have an entity level target to retrofit and be 100% ready no later by 2035 if not earlier.

Given the constraints mentioned above, the timeline to retrofit to 100% hydrogen-ready for Singapore CCGTs will be based on EMA’s forward guidance, e.g. through Singapore’s Emission Standards, when EMA requires CCGTs to be retrofitted to 100% hydrogen-ready with baseload compatibility with natural gas.

At COP26 in Glasgow, the Prime Minister announced an enhanced target of carbon neutrality by 2050 and reaffirmed the net-zero goal by 2065, with the potential to raise emission reductions to 40% by 2030, contingent on adequate international support 6 .
In November 2022, Thailand Second Updated NDC 7 and the revised LT-LEDs 8 , committing to a 30% GHG reduction by 2030, with an enhanced ambition of up to 40% under favorable conditions.
According to the draft National Energy Plan, at least 50% of new power generation will be renewable by 2050, with solar and wind projected to contribute 65% of total electricity generation by 2060.
With full support, this would represent a 60% reduction from 2019 levels, potentially aligning Thailand with a pathway to limit global temperature rise to 1.5°C.

Criteria are recorded as type 'eligible_projects', not 'substantial_contribution': the document states what may be financed, not the performance an activity must meet.

The source PDF is a scan with no text layer and no French OCR model was available, so the tables were transcribed by reading the page images. Threshold wording is verbatim; some project lines are condensed — see raw/UMOA_transcription.md.
The freight-transport figures are quoted by the Circulaire from the Climate Bonds Standard, not set by AMF-UMOA itself.
Social projects carry no climate objective in the source table; they are recorded with objective='social'.
Jurisdictions: UMOA has 8 member states. The Circulaire applies union-wide.

framework.name: South African Green Finance Taxonomy
framework.issuer: National Treasury — Taxonomy Working Group, under South Africa's Sustainable Finance Initiative

objectives.local: Sustainable use of water and marine resources

assessment.method: A seven-step alignment process: … Step 4 meet the applicable Technical Screening Criteria; Step 5 Principle 2 — do no significant harm to any other objective; Step 6 Principle 3 — comply with Minimum Social Safeguards; Step 7 conclude on taxonomic alignment.
assessment.generic_dnsh: Appendices A and D-F give generic DNSH criteria per objective, and Appendix C the Minimum Social Safeguards.

notes: Structurally the closest of this group to the EU Taxonomy: substantial contribution + DNSH + minimum social safeguards, with generic DNSH criteria per objective in appendices.

Many thresholds are visibly lifted from the EU delegated acts (for example the '10% most efficient installations in 2016 and 2017' benchmark). Where a value carries a comma, read it as the EU does — a decimal point.
The document uses South Africa's own SIC codes rather than ISIC.

ACTIVITY LIST NOT YET EXTRACTED. The document's activity table could not be recovered from the flattened PDF text to a standard this dataset is willing to state as fact, so 'activities' is empty on purpose. What IS here is every numeric threshold sentence found in the document, quoted verbatim with its metric and unit, and marked as a criterion, as national-policy context, or as ambiguous. Quote only the ones marked 'criterion' as taxonomy thresholds.

Activity list now populated: 44 activities, each with its substantial-contribution criteria, its Metric and Threshold block, and its DNSH block. South Africa converted the EU's comma decimals to points when it adopted the EU values (EU 0,722 tCO2e/t appears here as 0.722), so this framework's separator really is a point — unlike Sri Lanka, which kept the comma.

The document states that principles and standards for substantially contributing to SOCIAL objectives were found to be needed, but the underlying tools and data were not ready, so social objectives are recommended for future development and are NOT in this edition.

Minimising process emissions through energy efficiency improvements and switch to alternative fuels and electricity with lower emissions than grid electricity promoting the reduction of the clinker to cement ration and the use of alternative clinkers and binders can contribute to the mitigation objective. Mitigation measures should be incorporated into a single investment plan within a determined time frame (5 or 10 years) that outlines how each of the measures in combination with others will in combination enable the activity to meet the threshold defined below actions.

criteria.text: Manufacture of Aluminium

Climate Change Mitigation Objective The manufacturing of aluminium is a highly energy intensive process. The CO 2 emissions related to the production of aluminium are primarily scope 2 emissions as defined by the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (i.e. from the generation of the electricity used). Aluminium manufacturing should rely on low carbon electricity and reduced direct emissions. Furthermore, all aluminium recycling is eligible due to significantly lower emissions than primary production. Mitigation measures should be incorporated into a single investment plan within a determined time frame (5 or 10 years) that outlines how each of the measures in combination with others will in combination enable the activity to meet the threshold defined below actions.

The activity manufactures one of the following: a. primary aluminium where the economic activity complies with two of the following criteria until 2025 and with all of the following criteria after 2025: i. the GHG emissions do not exceed 1.484 34 tCO2 per ton of aluminium manufactured 35 : ii. the average carbon intensity for the indirect GHG emissions 36 does not exceed 100g CO2e/kWh; iii. the electricity consumption for the manufacturing process does not exceed 15.5 MWh/t Al. b. secondary aluminium. - Climate Change Adaptation Depending on the primary objective of the activity, refer to Section 8 Screening criteria for activities making a substantial contribution to climate change adaptation. Users of the Taxonomy should identify and explain which criteria they are responding to.

assessment - The main potential significant harm to other environmental objectives from the manufacture of aluminium is associated with: • The potential for significant air emission impacts: perfluorocarbons, fluoride gases, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and particulate matter (e.g. unused cryolite). Hydrogen fluorides can be toxic to vegetation; • The toxic, corrosive and reactive nature of waste generated by the used linings (cathodes) from the electrolytic cells (known as spent pot lining (SPL)). Dissolved fluorides and cyanides from the SPL material can create significant environmental impacts including groundwater contamination and pollution of local watercourses; • The ability (or lacking thereof) of aluminium manufacturing plants to incorporate aluminium scrap (including scrap from their own manufacturing processes) in the production process; and • The potential to impact ecosystems as a result of the land footprint of the site and from polluting emissions. criteria.text: Manufacture of Hydrogen

Climate Change Mitigation Objective The manufacturing of hydrogen is a highly carbon-intensive activity within the chemical industry. Reducing the emissions from the manufacturing activity itself can positively contribute to the mitigation objectives.

The activity complies with the life-cycle GHG emissions savings requirement of 73.4% for hydrogen [resulting in 3tCO2eq/tH2] and 70% for hydrogen-based synthetic fuels relative to a fossil fuel comparator of 94g CO2e/MJ. Life cycle GHG emissions savings are calculated using the methodology referred to in ISO 14067:2018 or ISO 14064-1:2018. Quantified life-cycle GHG emission savings are verified by an independent third party. Where the CO 2 emitted from the manufacturing process is captured, the CO 2 is transported and stored underground, in accordance with the technical screening criteria set out in in Section 3.4.11 and 3.4.12. Climate Change Adaptation Depending on the primary objective of the activity, refer to Section 8 Screening criteria for activities making a substantial contribution to climate change adaptation. Users of the Taxonomy should identify and explain which criteria they are responding to.

assessment The main potential significant harm to other environmental objectives from the manufacture of hydrogen is, in practical terms, inseparable from the potential for significant harm created by the hydrocarbon refining activity more generally and is associated with: • Polluting emissions to air (in the case of hydrogen production via electrolysis, there is an indirect environmental impact associated with the generation of electricity); • Water used for cooling might lead to local resource depletion, dependent of the local scarcity of water resources; and • The generation of wastes (e.g. spent catalysts and by-products of the various physical and chemical treatment processes used in purifying the hydrogen produced via hydrocarbon processing). Quantified life-cycle GHG emission savings are verified by an independent third party. criteria.text: Manufacture of plastics in primary form

Climate Change Mitigation Objective The manufacturing of plastics is associated with significant life cycle CO 2 emissions. There are many types of plastics which are used in the production of multiple end products. The Taxonomy seeks to avoid including manufacture of products that do not have a positive impact in mitigation. Disposable plastic products are highly energy inefficient and undermine efforts to contribute to mitigation. In this context, plastic manufacturing should be considered when at least 90% of the final plastic is not used for single use consumer products. This should be confirmed from science based research/studies etc. Mitigation measures should be incorporated into a single investment plan within a determined time frame (5 or 10 years) that outlines how each of the measures in combination with others will in combination enable the activity to meet the threshold defined below actions.

The plastic in primary form is one of the following: a. fully manufactured by mechanical recycling of plastic waste; b. fully manufactured by chemical recycling of plastic waste and the life-cycle GHG emissions of the manufactured plastic, excluding any calculated benefit from the production of fuels, are lower than the life-cycle GHG emissions of the equivalent primary plastic manufactured from fossil fuel feedstock. Life-cycle GHG emissions are calculated using ISO 14067:2018 or ISO 14064- 1:2018. Quantified life-cycle GHG emissions are verified by an independent third party. c. derived wholly or partially from renewable feedstock 72 and its life-cycle GHG emissions are lower than the life-cycle GHG emissions of the equivalent plastics in primary form manufactured from fossil fuel feedstock. Life-cycle GHG emissions are calculated using ISO 14067:2018 or ISO 14064- 1:2018. Quantified life-cycle GHG emissions are verified by an independent third party. Food or feed crops are not used as bio-based feedstock for the manufacture of plastic in primary form. Climate Change Adaptation Depending on the primary objective of the activity, refer to Section 8 Screening criteria for activities making a substantial contribution to climate change adaptation. Users of the Taxonomy should identify and explain which criteria they are responding to.

criteria.text: Water collection, storage, distribution, treatment and supply with high energy efficiency of the system.

Climate Change Mitigation Objective Substantial contribution to GHG emissions savings through low specific energy consumption in the water collection, treatment and supply system. By 2025 the feasibility of Option 2, in particular with regard to the intended incentive for substantial energy efficiency improvements in water supply systems, will be assessed.

The front-to-end water collection, storage, distribution, treatment and supply system is eligible provided that it’s performance in terms of energy consumption per cubic meter of final water supply is high or substantially improved. Eligibility is demonstrated by adherence to one of two optional thresholds: • Option 1: The front-to-end water supply, storage and distribution system has a high degree of energy efficiency characterized by an average energy consumption of the system (including abstraction, treatment and distribution) of 0.5 kwh per cubic meter billed/unbilled authorized water supply or less 76 . • Option 2: The energy efficiency of the front-to-end water supply storage and distribution system is increased substantially by decreasing the average energy consumption of the system by at least 20% (including abstraction, treatment and distribution; measured in kwh per cubic meter billed/unbilled authorized water supply); Or • by closing the gap between the actual leakage of the water supply storage and distribution network and a given target value of low leakage by at least 20%.
